headline: Symmetry is when parts mirror each other—a signal of health, beauty, and order across nature and art
universal_truth: Balance creates beauty; what matches suggests wholeness and health
fun_facts: Humans prefer symmetrical faces—symmetry signals genetic health and developmental stability
Most animals are bilaterally symmetrical, but starfish and jellyfish show radial symmetry
Snowflakes have six-fold symmetry because of how water molecules bond when freezing
discussion_questions: Why is symmetry so universally beautiful?
When is asymmetry more interesting than symmetry?
What areas of your life feel balanced versus unbalanced?

hook.script: Your face is roughly symmetrical—left matches right. Butterflies are symmetrical. Buildings are symmetrical. We find symmetry beautiful and use it in art and architecture. But why? What makes matching halves so universally appealing?

cliff.script: Symmetry appears everywhere in nature and human design. We find it beautiful without being taught to. Why does the brain respond so positively to symmetry?
cliff.prompt: Why do we find symmetry beautiful?

options.text: Symmetry signals health and order—asymmetry often indicates disease, damage, or disorder, so we evolved to prefer symmetry
options.response: Yes. Symmetrical bodies suggest healthy development. Asymmetry can signal illness or genetic problems. Our preference for symmetry may be an evolved health detector.

options.text: Symmetry is simpler for the brain to process
options.response: Processing ease is part of it, but the evolutionary signal of health matters too...

fact1.title: Health Signal
fact1.script: Developmental problems often cause asymmetry. Parasites, diseases, and genetic issues can disrupt balanced growth. Symmetry says: 'I developed correctly.' That's why symmetrical faces are rated as more attractive—they signal health.

fact2.title: Types of Symmetry
fact2.script: Bilateral symmetry: left-right mirror (humans, butterflies). Radial symmetry: multiple lines from center (starfish, flowers). Rotational symmetry: looks same when rotated (snowflakes). Different symmetries serve different purposes.

fact3.title: Breaking Symmetry
fact3.script: Perfect symmetry can be boring. Artists often introduce slight asymmetry for interest—a face turned, a building with one tower. Dynamic balance—asymmetry that still feels balanced—can be more engaging than perfect mirroring.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Balance creates beauty. Symmetry teaches that what matches suggests wholeness and health. But don't fear asymmetry—sometimes breaking the pattern creates something more interesting.

outro.script: That's Day 175. Tomorrow, we'll explore making flat things look deep—perspective. Until then, notice symmetry and asymmetry around you—in faces, buildings, nature, and your own life balance.

growTrack.title: Balance Check - Symmetry in Life
growTrack.learning_objective: Evaluate balance in different life areas
growTrack.activity: Draw a line down a page. On each side, list matching pairs in your life: work/rest, giving/receiving, social/solitude. Are they balanced? Where is healthy asymmetry, and where does imbalance create problems? Life needs dynamic balance.
